brain barrier consists of capillary endothelial cells and a 
membrane to protect the brain from toxins, which includes 
chemotherapies and other targeted drugs. The endothelial cells are 
fused together by proteins which restrict blood components from 
crossing through the barrier.  
 
Molecules within the barrier are responsible for angiogenesis (blood 
vessel growth) and signalling.  
 
Membrane proteins within the brain are known as uptake and efflux 
transporters. Downregulation of efflux transporter proteins can also 
create a more penetrable blood brain barrier.  
 
Understanding how to break down the barrier and finding supports 
that will help drugs to be safely delivered through it, are key factors in 
treating brain metastases, very few chemotherapy drugs cross the 
blood brain barrier.  
 
The endothelial cells contain transporters such as multi -drug resistant 
proteins MDRP1 -9, ABCG2 (also known as BBRP) and P -
Glycoprotein mediated efflux.  
 
17 
 Histone protein acylation modulators can impact on MDRP -1 to 
reduce drug resistance.  
Regulators of histone proteins include green tea EGCG, curcumin, 
quercetin, grape cyanidins, L Carnitine, sulforaphane, artichoke, 
silymarin from milk Thistle, Genistein and apigenin.  
 
ABCG2 is the protein responsible from stopping drug resistance in 
breast cancer. It is also known as BCRP.  
 
BCRP can be increased by indole 3 carbinol, green tea, resveratrol 
(not in post -menopausal women), Quercetin, and fruit and vegetables 
such as apples, grapes, onions, broccoli, and cabbage.  
 
P-Glycoprotein limits the bioavailability of drugs taken orally.  
It does this by pumping them back into the lumen (membrane of the 
intestine). This promotes drug elimination into the urine and the bile 
and protects organs such as the brain, testes and lymphocytes.
